summary: The note describes two St. Peter's Basilicas in Rome. Old St. Peter's, begun by Emperor Constantine the Great between 319 and 333 AD, was a basilica shaped like a tau cross, over 103.6 metres long, built over the believed burial site of St. Peter and holding burials of most popes up to the 15th century. The current St. Peter's Basilica is an Italian Renaissance church in Vatican City, and the name Old St. Peter's is used for its predecessor to distinguish them.
one_line: Overview of Old St. Peter's Basilica, Constantine's 4th-century church in Rome, and the current Renaissance St. Peter's Basilica in Vatican City.
key_facts: Old St. Peter's Basilica was a 4th-century church begun by the Emperor Constantine the Great between 319 and 333 AD.
Old St. Peter's Basilica was of typical basilical form with a wide nave, two aisles on each side, and an apsidal end.
Old St. Peter's Basilica had a transept or bema, giving the building the shape of a tau cross.
Old St. Peter's Basilica was over 103.6 metres (340 ft) long.
The entrance of Old St. Peter's Basilica was preceded by a large colonnaded atrium.
Old St. Peter's Basilica was built over the small shrine believed to mark the burial place of St. Peter.
Old St. Peter's Basilica contained a very large number of burials and memorials, including those of most of the popes from St. Peter to the 15th century.
Like all of the earliest churches in Rome, Old St. Peter's Basilica and its successor had the entrance to the east and the apse at the west end.
The name Old St. Peter's Basilica has been used for its predecessor since the construction of the current basilica, to distinguish the two buildings.
The Papal Basilica of St. Peter in the Vatican, also called St. Peter's Basilica (Latin: Basilica Sancti Petri), is an Italian Renaissance church.
The current St. Peter's Basilica is located in Vatican City, the papal enclave within the city of Rome.
